title: Sociology and Social Change
text:
Monday gave us the fundamentals
Structure and agency. Social facts. Troubles and issues. Social construction. Social order and social change.
Today: three perspectives that ask different questions of the same problem, and the core concepts that explain how a person comes to participate at all.

Time: 2 minutes. Source: Chapter 9, §§9.4–9.6. Reconnect to Week 6: paradigms shaped what counts as evidence; perspectives shape what counts as the question.
Pacing. Full deck is 56 minutes; the core path is 44. Slides marked “If time is short, skip this slide” are the drop list: roles and identities, socialization-can-exclude, and community-based conservation. Protect Box 9.2 and the two socialization slides — they are Friday item 3.


Source: Chapter 9, §§9.4–9.6

title: Sociology and Social Change
text:
Today’s question
Three sociologists look at the same declining participation. What does each one ask?

Time: 1 minute. Source: Chapter 9, §9.4 and Table 9.1. Write it on the board. Friday does not require students to pick a perspective, but items 2 and 3 reward a student who can hear which one a claim is coming from.


Source: Chapter 9, §9.4 and Table 9.1

title: Sociology and Social Change
section: What you should be able to do
text:
What you should be able to do
By the end of today, you should be able to:

distinguish functionalism, conflict, and symbolic interactionism;
explain roles and identities as socially constructed;
explain socialization through agent, target, and context; and
use community and stratification to say who is served and who is not.


Time: 1 minute. Source: Chapter 9, §§9.4–9.6.4. These map onto Friday’s items 2, 3, and 4.


Source: Chapter 9, §§9.4–9.6.4

title: Sociology and Social Change
text:
Three perspectives
Functionalism · Conflict · Symbolic interactionism

Time: 1 minute. Source: Chapter 9, §9.4 and Table 9.1.


Source: Chapter 9, §9.4 and Table 9.1

title: Sociology and Social Change
text:
What each one asks








Perspective
View of society
The question it asks




Functionalism
Interdependent institutions, each with a function, maintaining the whole
How do the parts of this system relate and produce this outcome?


Conflict
Structure emerging from competition for resources and power; winners and losers
Who wins, who loses, how did that emerge, and what structures sustain it?


Symbolic interactionism
Meaning built and negotiated through everyday interaction
How do people construct the meaning of this thing through interaction?




Time: 6 minutes. Source: Chapter 9, §9.4 and Table 9.1. Work one problem across all three columns — declining access is ideal. Functionalism: what function did the walk-in program serve in the system? Conflict: who gained access when residents lost it? Interactionism: what does “being a hunter here” mean now? None is the correct one; each is a different question.


Source: Chapter 9, §9.4 and Table 9.1

title: Sociology and Social Change
text:
Roles and identities
Roles are social positions carrying expectations for behavior. Identity is the meaning a person attaches to themselves based on how they understand and prioritize those roles.

Most of us expect to occupy the role of “parent.” Far fewer occupy “angler,” “hunter,” “birdwatcher,” or “falconer.”
The meanings and expectations of a prominent role are more widely shared than those of an uncommon one.


Time: 4 minutes. Source: Chapter 9, §9.6.1. The management payoff: hunter identities are shaped by material factors too — weapon type, method, target species — plus social class, residency, and particular landscapes. That is why agencies should segment hunter typologies rather than treat participants as one uniform group. “Hunters support this” is usually a claim that has not been checked.
If time is short, skip this slide. The thread survives without it.


Source: Chapter 9, §9.6.1

title: Sociology and Social Change
text:
Socialization
How people learn the beliefs, values, norms, and behaviors of their culture.

Time: 1 minute. Source: Chapter 9, §9.6.2. Open by noting that fish and wildlife management relies heavily on voluntary compliance — so how people are socialized into expected standards is not a side topic.


Source: Chapter 9, §9.6.2

title: Sociology and Social Change
text:
Agent, target, context

Agent — the person or institution doing the socializing.
Target — the person being socialized.
Context — the setting in which it happens.

Primary socialization happens through parents in childhood. Secondary socialization happens through peers, teachers, extended family, media, and institutions.

Time: 4 minutes. Source: Chapter 9, §9.6.2 and Box 9.2. These three variables are the analytic tool for Friday’s item 3. Have students name the agent, target, and context in their own introduction to any outdoor activity — without requiring anyone to share.


Source: Chapter 9, §9.6.2 and Box 9.2

title: Sociology and Social Change
text:
Box 9.2 — what actually predicts participation
National survey data on three variables: gender, rural upbringing, and whether the respondent’s father hunted.

82% of males with a hunting father had tried hunting — and rural versus urban upbringing made no difference (81% vs. 83%).
For females with a hunting father, the effect was modest: 27%.
For females without a hunting father: 6%, with rural upbringing making no difference.


The presence of a hunting agent in the household mattered more than the rural or urban context in which socialization took place.


Time: 6 minutes. Source: Chapter 9, Box 9.2. Present these as findings about socialization mechanisms, not as claims about who ought to hunt. The striking result is that a primary agent made context nearly irrelevant.


Source: Chapter 9, Box 9.2

title: Sociology and Social Change
text:
When does rural upbringing matter?
Exactly one case: males who grew up rural without hunting fathers were far more likely to have tried hunting (59%) than urban males without hunting fathers (34%).

Rural upbringing fosters participation mainly by standing in for absent primary agents — other family, friends, or institutions step in where the behavior is widely seen as normative.


Time: 5 minutes. Source: Chapter 9, Box 9.2. This is the slide that makes Friday’s Response C intelligible: if secondary agents substitute for absent primary ones, then a program that supplies a mentor is intervening on the actual mechanism. No corresponding effect was observed for females, which the chapter connects to how normative the behavior is for each group.


Source: Chapter 9, Box 9.2

title: Sociology and Social Change
text:
Socialization can also exclude
Carini and Weber examined how angling magazines socialize women into the sport. They found women were:

underrepresented relative to their actual participation;
depicted in stereotypical roles;
usually accompanied by men; and
overtly sexualized.


When images reinforce a male-centric social space, people may not see themselves as suitable members of the group.


Time: 4 minutes. Source: Chapter 9, §9.6.2. Media is a secondary socialization agent, and it operates whether or not an agency intends it to. Keep this analytic; the point is the mechanism, not an indictment of a magazine.
If time is short, skip this slide. The thread survives without it.


Source: Chapter 9, §9.6.2

title: Sociology and Social Change
text:
Community
The intermediary space between the individual and broader society.

Time: 1 minute. Source: Chapter 9, §9.6.3.


Source: Chapter 9, §9.6.3

title: Sociology and Social Change
text:
Three elements of community

Local territory — a specific physical setting.
Local society — the structures and institutions that meet local needs.
Social interaction — active engagement of people with one another.

A community facing an urgent issue can act in ways not predictable from its members’ individual attitudes — a local ordinance may be a collective compromise that reflects nobody’s average view.

Time: 4 minutes. Source: Chapter 9, §9.6.3. Note the second element for Friday: when the institutions that met local needs disappear, the community can persist in territory while losing the structures that carried a practice.


Source: Chapter 9, §9.6.3

title: Sociology and Social Change
text:
Community-based conservation is not automatic
Locally designed institutions can outperform centralized management. But success depends on context and the robustness of the process.

Credibility: do short-term local interests override broader goals?
Capacity: technical expertise, management skill, finances, political access.
Power: collaboration can be derailed when elite factions hold disproportionate influence.


Without these assets, community-based approaches can reinforce existing inequalities rather than correct them.


Time: 4 minutes. Source: Chapter 9, §9.6.3. This is a direct callback to Week 5’s collaboration material. “Community-led” is not a synonym for “equitable,” and Friday’s item 4 asks who a recommendation does not serve.
If time is short, skip this slide. The thread survives without it.


Source: Chapter 9, §9.6.3

title: Sociology and Social Change
text:
Stratification and inequality
Stratification: the processes allocating resources and opportunities by hierarchical ranking or socially agreed criteria. Inequality: the uneven or unfair distribution that results.

The cost of equipment, transportation, and access can become prohibitive.
Agencies risk losing large segments of their user base who can no longer afford to participate.
Public trust thinking holds that wildlife is not owned by any group but held for the public benefit — which makes equity a trust obligation, not a preference.


Time: 4 minutes. Source: Chapter 9, §9.6.4. Close the loop to Week 5 explicitly: the funding structure that positions license buyers first is a stratification fact with a governance consequence. On Friday, the rise in leased-land nonresident hunts is the stratification evidence.


Source: Chapter 9, §9.6.4

title: Sociology and Social Change
text:
Pair rehearsal: name the perspective
With a partner, name the perspective behind each claim:

“The walk-in program held the access system together; when it shrank, everything downstream failed.”
“Out-of-state lease clients gained the access that local residents lost.”
“‘Heritage’ means something different now than it did when my father said it.”


Time: 5 minutes. Source: Chapter 9, §9.4. Answers: functionalism, conflict, symbolic interactionism. All three claims are available from Friday’s case brief, and the third is the social-construction item in Friday’s item 3.


Source: Chapter 9, §9.4

title: Sociology and Social Change
text:
Friday
Read the Week 08 Case Brief: Who Still Hunts Cedar County? before class. Everything you need is in it.
Licenses down 44% in twenty years. County population nearly flat. Farm operations down from 1,290 to 610. Posted acres up from 61,000 to 219,000.

Time: 2 minutes. Source: Chapter 9, §§9.3–9.6. Tell students the roles this week are social structure lead, meaning and identity lead, and community and consequences lead. Repeat the frame: the county is fictional, no claim is made about any real community, and nobody is asked about their own background. Note that the $260,000 budget does not fit any two responses together.


Source: Chapter 9, §§9.3–9.6

title: Sociology and Social Change
text:
Close

A response aimed at individual preference cannot fix a problem produced by structural change. Diagnosing which one you have is the whole job.


Time: 1 minute. Source: Chapter 9, §9.7. Preview Week 9: economics, where those same distributional questions get prices attached.


Source: Chapter 9, §9.7

title: Psychology and Human Behavior
text:
Monday gave us a diagnosis
Cognition, conation, affect. Person and situation. The specificity principle.
Today those become frameworks — the tools that turn a diagnosis into a strategy someone could fund and evaluate.

Time: 2 minutes. Source: Chapter 8, §8.4. Remind students that the specificity principle from Box 8.5 is the reason TACT exists; they are the same idea at two levels of abstraction.
Pacing. Full deck is 53 minutes; the core path is 45. Slides marked “If time is short, skip this slide” are the drop list: motivation/satisfaction and self-determination theory. Protect TACT, the reasoned action approach, and the pair rehearsal — they map directly onto Friday items 1 and 3.


Source: Chapter 8, §8.4

title: Psychology and Human Behavior
text:
Today’s question
What has to be true before a person performs a specific conservation behavior?

Time: 1 minute. Source: Chapter 8, §8.4.3. Write it on the board. Every framework today is an answer to this question from a different angle.


Source: Chapter 8, §8.4.3

title: Psychology and Human Behavior
section: What you should be able to do
text:
What you should be able to do
By the end of today, you should be able to:

define a target behavior using TACT;
apply the reasoned action approach — attitudes, perceived norms, perceived behavioral control;
explain collective action and why a perceived norm changes what an individual does; and
use affect, motivation, and satisfaction to explain a behavior the other frameworks miss.


Time: 1 minute. Source: Chapter 8, §§8.4.2–8.4.5. These four map onto Friday’s four response items in order.


Source: Chapter 8, §§8.4.2–8.4.5

title: Psychology and Human Behavior
text:
Define the behavior first
You cannot manage, measure, or evaluate a behavior you have not specified.

Time: 1 minute. Source: Chapter 8, §8.4.3.


Source: Chapter 8, §8.4.3

title: Psychology and Human Behavior
text:
TACT









Letter
Question
Weak
Strong




Target
What or whom?
“the environment”
live wells, bilge, and drain plug


Action
Do what, exactly?
“be responsible”
drain them


Context
Where, under what conditions?
“in general”
before leaving the north ramp


Time
When, how often, for how long?
“someday”
every trip, 2027 open-water season




“Boaters should care more about invasive species” fails all four. It cannot be observed, so it cannot be managed.


Time: 6 minutes. Source: Chapter 8, §8.4.3 and Box 8.5. Do this live: take a vague goal from the class and force all four columns. Then ask who would observe it and where — if nobody can answer that, the behavior is still not specified. Friday’s item 1 is exactly this exercise.


Source: Chapter 8, §8.4.3 and Box 8.5

title: Psychology and Human Behavior
text:
The reasoned action approach
Behavioral intention is the most immediate predictor of behavior. Three things shape it:

Attitudes — the person’s own evaluation of the behavior.
Perceived norms — the social pressure to perform or avoid it.
Perceived behavioral control (self-efficacy) — belief in one’s ability to carry it out successfully.


Time: 6 minutes. Source: Chapter 8, §8.4.3. Stress that these are three separate levers. A favorable attitude with no self-efficacy produces nothing; so does high self-efficacy against a hostile norm. This is why “raise awareness” campaigns fail when awareness was never the binding constraint.


Source: Chapter 8, §8.4.3

title: Psychology and Human Behavior
text:
Which lever is actually broken?

Attitude is fine, norm is fine, control is low → make the behavior easier, teach the skill, remove the time cost.


Attitude is fine, control is fine, norm is low → make others’ behavior visible; recruit the groups people belong to.


Attitude is the problem → this is the rarest case in conservation, and the one most campaigns assume.


Time: 5 minutes. Source: Chapter 8, §8.4.3. Reveal one at a time. This slide is the practical payoff of the whole week: the diagnosis determines the intervention, and getting it wrong wastes the budget. Friday’s case brief is built so that the third box is demonstrably not the problem.


Source: Chapter 8, §8.4.3

title: Psychology and Human Behavior
text:
Collective action
Some behaviors only make sense if others are doing them too.

Time: 1 minute. Source: Chapter 8, §8.4.2.


Source: Chapter 8, §8.4.2

title: Psychology and Human Behavior
text:
Individual factors and collective factors
The collective interest model holds that behavior is influenced by individual factors and collective factors together.
In the Montana bear-attractant work (Box 8.4):

Different attractant-securing behaviors were associated with different suites of individual factors.
Collective factors were influential across the board.
Landowners who believed their neighbors were securing attractants, and expected them to keep doing so, were 30% to 100% more likely to secure their own.


Time: 6 minutes. Source: Chapter 8, Box 8.4. The most consistent individual predictor was biocentric belief, but the collective effect was the one that held across every behavior. Practitioners responded by changing the messaging to convey normative information, reduce feelings of isolation, and invest in professionals who start conversations among landowners.


Source: Chapter 8, Box 8.4

title: Psychology and Human Behavior
text:
Why this changes the intervention

If a person’s behavior depends on what they believe others are doing, then a message about the harm of the problem is aimed at the wrong variable.

A perceived norm can be wrong. People routinely underestimate how many others are complying — and act on the underestimate.

Time: 4 minutes. Source: Chapter 8, §8.4.2. This distinction matters on Friday: a survey item asking “do most others drain their boats?” measures a perceived norm, not a compliance rate. Groups that treat it as a measured rate have made an error the brief warns about.


Source: Chapter 8, §8.4.2

title: Psychology and Human Behavior
text:
Affect: emotions are not decoration
Emotions influence perception, judgment, memory, and behavior. They are psychological and physiological responses to events, situations, or stimuli.

Seeing a robin at a feeder, or a raccoon at a trash can, can evoke anything from appreciation and awe to fear or disgust.
In a deer-management study, emotions influenced the acceptability of management options.


Time: 4 minutes. Source: Chapter 8, §8.4.4. Affect is a relative newcomer in this field, which is why it is often missing from agency analysis. Note the management consequence: emotion shapes not only behavior but whether a proposed action is seen as acceptable at all. Resentment toward an agency is affect, and it is actionable evidence.


Source: Chapter 8, §8.4.4

title: Psychology and Human Behavior
text:
Motivation and satisfaction
Motivation is why people act. Satisfaction is what they get out of it.
Decker and Connelly’s three orientations:

Affiliative — social interaction and bonding.
Achievement — reaching a performance goal.
Appreciative — peace, belonging, stress reduction.


Time: 4 minutes. Source: Chapter 8, §8.4.5. The management consequence is that agencies must manage more than bag limits: they manage experiential outcomes. Two people performing the identical behavior may be seeking entirely different things, and a program that serves one may not serve the other.
If time is short, skip this slide. The thread survives without it.


Source: Chapter 8, §8.4.5

title: Psychology and Human Behavior
text:
Self-determination theory
Motivation is driven by three basic psychological needs:

Autonomy — feeling in control of one’s own actions.
Competence — feeling effective in an environment.
Relatedness — connection with others.


A program that tells people what to do, implies they are doing it wrong, and isolates them, undercuts all three at once.


Time: 4 minutes. Source: Chapter 8, §8.4.5. When conservation programs meet these needs, participants show higher intrinsic motivation. Connect to Friday: an enforcement-only framing can damage autonomy and relatedness even when the rule itself is correct.
If time is short, skip this slide. The thread survives without it.


Source: Chapter 8, §8.4.5

title: Psychology and Human Behavior
text:
Pair rehearsal: match the lever
With a partner, name the framework and the lever you would pull:

“There’s a line of eight boats and a guy in a hurry behind me. I’m not holding that up for ten minutes.”


“On the tournament circuit everybody decons. You’d get talked about if you didn’t.”


“Every sign out here is written like we did something wrong.”


Time: 5 minutes. Source: Chapter 8, §§8.4.2–8.4.4. Answers: perceived behavioral control plus a situational constraint; perceived norm, strongly positive; affect, with a self-determination reading available. All three quotations are in Friday’s case brief, so this is direct rehearsal for items 2 and 3.


Source: Chapter 8, §§8.4.2–8.4.4

title: Psychology and Human Behavior
text:
Friday
Read the Week 07 Case Brief: The Thornapple Lake Decontamination Problem before class. Everything you need is in it.
A $180,000 campaign changed nothing — because 92% of boaters already agreed invasive mussels are harmful, before and after.

Time: 2 minutes. Source: Chapter 8, §§8.4–8.4.5. Tell students the roles this week are target behavior lead, person factors lead, and situation and norms lead, and that the roster is published. Warn them that the $220,000 budget arithmetic is part of the grade.


Source: Chapter 8, §§8.4–8.4.5

title: Psychology and Human Behavior
text:
Close

A strategy that cannot name its target behavior, the lever it is pulling, and the indicator that would show it working is not a strategy. It is a hope.


Time: 1 minute. Source: Chapter 8, §8.5. Preview Week 8: the same decline problem viewed from sociology, where the unit of analysis stops being the individual.


Source: Chapter 8, §8.5

title: Disciplines and Paradigms
section: The method is never the whole story
text:
The method is never the whole story
On Monday, we used disciplines to see different parts of a management problem.
Today we ask the prior question: What assumptions lead a team to call one kind of evidence persuasive, relevant, or sufficient?

Time: 2 minutes. Source: Chapter 7, §7.3. Use a familiar contrast: a survey can show a broad pattern; it cannot, on its own, show how every community makes meaning of that pattern. Neither fact makes one method universally superior.


Source: Chapter 7, §7.3

title: Disciplines and Paradigms
section: By the end of class, you can
text:
By the end of class, you can

distinguish ontology, epistemology, methodology, and axiology;
compare how paradigms shape questions and evidence; and
select a defensible combination of approaches for a contested decision.


Time: 2 minutes. Source: Chapter 7, §§7.3–7.3.3. These objectives prepare students to identify assumptions and then use them in a management case.


Source: Chapter 7, §§7.3–7.3.3

title: Disciplines and Paradigms
section: A paradigm is a working worldview
text:
A paradigm is a working worldview
It shapes what a researcher takes to be real, how knowledge can be developed, which methods fit, and what purposes should guide inquiry.

Time: 1 minute. Source: Chapter 7, §7.3.2. Make the term less intimidating: students already make assumptions when they decide that a number, story, map, or meeting should carry weight in a decision.


Source: Chapter 7, §7.3.2

title: Disciplines and Paradigms
section: Four questions sit underneath a research design
text:
Four questions sit underneath a research design



Foundation
Plain-language question




Ontology
What is real here?


Epistemology
What can we know, and how?


Methodology
What process can produce credible knowledge?


Axiology
What values and responsibilities guide the inquiry?




Source: Chapter 7, §7.3.1.


Time: 5 minutes. Source: Chapter 7, §7.3.1. Give a deer-management example. One team may treat attitude as a measurable construct; another may focus on the different meanings residents attach to deer. Both must still explain how their approach produces credible knowledge and how it will be used.


Source: Chapter 7, §7.3.1

title: Disciplines and Paradigms
section: Axiology is why “value-free” is not the whole answer
text:
Axiology is why “value-free” is not the whole answer
Researchers and managers make choices about:

which problems are worth studying;
whose experiences and knowledge are included;
what harms to avoid; and
how findings should be used.

Naming those choices does not make research less rigorous. It makes its responsibilities more visible.

Source: Chapter 7, §7.3.1.


Time: 3 minutes. Source: Chapter 7, §7.3.1. Connect to Weeks 4–5: a monitoring system is built around objectives, and governance determines who helps set them. Axiology is not an excuse to ignore evidence; it clarifies what evidence is being sought and why.


Source: Chapter 7, §7.3.1

title: Disciplines and Paradigms
section: The same wolf issue can generate different rigorous questions
text:
The same wolf issue can generate different rigorous questions







Starting point
A question it makes possible




Measure a pattern
What percentage of residents supports recovery?


Interpret meaning
How do communities describe what wolves represent?


Examine power
Whose voices are absent from recovery decisions?


Solve a problem
What evidence mix can support a workable decision?




Source: Chapter 7, §7.3.2.


Time: 4 minutes. Source: Chapter 7, §7.3.2. These are adapted from the chapter’s key point. Ask students which question a statewide survey answers best and which require a different design. Do not characterize any one question as the “correct” starting point in all contexts.


Source: Chapter 7, §7.3.2

title: Disciplines and Paradigms
section: Positivism: measure a reality that exists independently
text:
Positivism: measure a reality that exists independently
Positivist work emphasizes observation, experimentation, and logical reasoning to identify patterns in a reality that is “out there” to be discovered.
Useful when: a question calls for careful measurement of a relationship or effect.
Watch for: meanings, histories, and unequal power may not be captured by measurement alone.

Source: Chapter 7, §7.3.2.1.


Time: 3 minutes. Source: Chapter 7, §7.3.2.1. Use the chapter’s message-test example: Does exposure to a particular habitat-restoration message increase support? Explain that a carefully designed experiment can be very strong for that bounded causal question.


Source: Chapter 7, §7.3.2.1

title: Disciplines and Paradigms
section: Post-positivism: measure carefully and stay revisable
text:
Post-positivism: measure carefully and stay revisable
Post-positivism still values systematic empirical inquiry, but treats knowledge as provisional because observation, measurement, and interpretation are imperfect.
It invites transparent limits: sampling error, uncertainty, bias, and plausible alternative explanations.

Source: Chapter 7, §7.3.2.2.


Time: 3 minutes. Source: Chapter 7, §7.3.2.2. Tie this to monitoring: a survey estimate of support for chronic-wasting-disease actions is useful, but it does not represent every resident perfectly or eliminate the need to revisit a decision as conditions change.


Source: Chapter 7, §7.3.2.2

title: Disciplines and Paradigms
section: Interpretivism: examine how people make meaning
text:
Interpretivism: examine how people make meaning
People’s experiences, cultures, histories, and contexts shape what a species or management action means to them. Multiple perspectives are part of the object of inquiry—not simply noise around one number.

Time: 1 minute. Source: Chapter 7, §7.3.2.3. Transition to approaches where the goal is not a single average or one universal interpretation.


Source: Chapter 7, §7.3.2.3

title: Disciplines and Paradigms
section: Interpretive evidence is systematic, not “just stories”
text:
Interpretive evidence is systematic, not “just stories”
Interviews, focus groups, participant observation, and narrative analysis can be designed carefully to examine how people construct meaning.
For wolf recovery, an interpretive study might ask how ranchers, Tribal members, agency staff, and urban residents each describe wolves and their management.
The goal is to understand context and differences in meaning—not to force them into a single account.

Source: Chapter 7, §7.3.2.3.


Time: 4 minutes. Source: Chapter 7, §7.3.2.3. Connect to the Arizona and commercial-fisher examples from Week 4: qualitative evidence can identify a blind spot in a measurement system. Rigor comes from transparent design and interpretation, not from pretending a lived experience is a percentage.


Source: Chapter 7, §7.3.2.3

title: Disciplines and Paradigms
section: Critical approaches ask how power shapes knowledge
text:
Critical approaches ask how power shapes knowledge
Critical inquiry examines how history, inequality, marginalization, and disenfranchisement affect whose knowledge is treated as legitimate and who experiences the consequences of a decision.
It carries an explicit commitment to justice, empowerment, and social change.

Source: Chapter 7, §7.3.2.4.


Time: 4 minutes. Source: Chapter 7, §7.3.2.4. Connect directly to Week 5: a participation process can appear inclusive while still withholding influence. Ask what evidence would reveal historical exclusion from a wildlife decision, and what a team would owe people once it recognized that exclusion.


Source: Chapter 7, §7.3.2.4

title: Disciplines and Paradigms
section: Pragmatism asks what combination can improve this decision
text:
Pragmatism asks what combination can improve this decision
Pragmatism treats knowledge as a tool for addressing a problem under real constraints: time, funding, politics, uncertainty, and implementation capacity.
It can combine survey patterns, interviews, and public testing of alternatives when that combination is useful and credible for the decision at hand.

Source: Chapter 7, §7.3.2.5.


Time: 4 minutes. Source: Chapter 7, §7.3.2.5. Avoid describing pragmatism as “anything goes.” It still requires a defensible fit between the question, evidence, feasibility, transparency, and decision process.


Source: Chapter 7, §7.3.2.5

title: Disciplines and Paradigms
section: Indigenous knowledge systems are not an add-on data source
text:
Indigenous knowledge systems are not an add-on data source
They are complete, place-based systems of knowledge, practice, relationship, responsibility, and governance.

Time: 1 minute. Source: Chapter 7, §7.3.3. State this plainly before any example. Do not collapse distinct Nations, communities, or knowledge systems into one generic category.


Source: Chapter 7, §7.3.3

title: Disciplines and Paradigms
section: Two-Eyed Seeing: work from the strengths of both eyes
text:
Two-Eyed Seeing: work from the strengths of both eyes
Etuaptmumk, often translated as Two-Eyed Seeing, is a Mi’kmaw concept that recognizes the value of Indigenous and Western knowledge systems while seeking respectful, meaningful partnership.
It is not a shortcut for extracting local observations into a Western project. It requires attention to relationships, sovereignty, and who guides the work.

Source: Chapter 7, §7.3.3.1.


Time: 4 minutes. Source: Chapter 7, §7.3.3.1. Pair this with the governance lecture: Tribal governments are sovereign decision-makers, not simply a stakeholder group. Emphasize that the concept names an orientation toward respectful partnership, not a universal method that others can claim without relationship or accountability.


Source: Chapter 7, §7.3.3.1

title: Disciplines and Paradigms
section: Case diagnosis: choose evidence without choosing sides
text:
Case diagnosis: choose evidence without choosing sides
Scenario: A state agency must revise a drought-season fishing closure. It has creel data, temperature records, and public comments, but hears that its current process misses subsistence and Tribal fishing perspectives.
In groups of three:

Name one question the agency must answer.
Name two kinds of evidence or knowledge that fit it.
State one process condition required for that evidence to be used responsibly.


Time: 8 minutes. Source: Chapter 7, §§7.3–7.3.3. Debrief toward fit and accountability. Good answers may include biological thresholds plus community experience, but require a process that recognizes sovereignty and does not ask one group to validate a decision already made.


Source: Chapter 7, §§7.3–7.3.3

Four rigorous proposals, one $180,000 budget, an eight-month deadline, and a late letter from a Tribal fisheries program setting a condition about who owns the knowledge.

Source: Chapter 7, §§7.3.1–7.3.3.
