Time: 3 minutes. Source: Chapter 6, §§6.1–6.2. Retrieve the prior connection: public-trust thinking asks managers to account for beneficiaries and future options; this chapter provides a routine for making and revising decisions.


Source: Chapter 6, §§6.1–6.2

title: Evidence, Framing, and Planning
text:
The central question

How does a human-dimensions orientation improve an evidence-based management decision?



At the most basic, it broadens both the evidence managers use and the outcomes they seek.


Time: 3 minutes. Source: Chapter 6, §§6.1–6.2. Ask students to listen for two threads today: evidence and problem framing.


Source: Chapter 6, §§6.1–6.2

title: Evidence, Framing, and Planning
text:
Evidence and framing
From a management question to a defensible plan.

Time: 1 minute. Transition slide.

title: Evidence, Framing, and Planning
section: A decision needs more than biological evidence
text:
A decision needs more than biological evidence


What is happening?

Biological or ecological conditions
Technical feasibility
Legal mandates


What should be done?

Economic feasibility
Social values
Public knowledge and experience



Key point: These evidence sources complement one another; none resolves every management question alone.


Time: 6 minutes. Source: Chapter 6, §6.2.1. Emphasize balance rather than a hierarchy of evidence.


Source: Chapter 6, §6.2.1

title: Evidence, Framing, and Planning
section: Evidence answers different parts of the decision
text:
Evidence answers different parts of the decision






Evidence type
A question it can help answer




Ecological and biological
What condition, risk, or response is occurring?


Social and economic
Who is affected, what matters, and what tradeoffs are feasible?


Legal and institutional
What authority, duty, or process applies?


Local and experiential
What place-based knowledge or implementation concern should shape the plan?






Source: Chapter 6, §6.2.1.


Time: 3 minutes. Evidence types answer different questions; the table does not create a hierarchy or claim each source resolves a decision alone.

title: Evidence, Framing, and Planning
text:
Four questions organize a decision


Why?
Why manage or conserve this resource?
Who?
Which publics, beneficiaries, and partners are involved?

What?
What impacts or outcomes are desired?
How?
How will the decision be made, carried out, and assessed?


Time: 6 minutes. Source: Chapter 6, §6.2. Ask students which question is easiest to overlook when a decision is framed only as a biological problem.


Source: Chapter 6, §6.2

title: Evidence, Framing, and Planning
section: Research and participation have different jobs
text:
Research and participation have different jobs
Research can describe conditions, relationships, and likely consequences.

Participation can reveal values, concerns, local knowledge, and acceptable tradeoffs.



Meaningful participation is more than a legal requirement. It needs a structured process, capable staff, and genuine integration of input.



Time: 5 minutes. Source: Chapter 6, §6.2.1. Connect to Grand Staircase–Escalante: participation affects both information and legitimacy.


Source: Chapter 6, §6.2.1

title: Evidence, Framing, and Planning
text:
Evidence-informed does not mean expert-only
Research can reduce uncertainty and test relationships. Participation can clarify values, lived experience, local knowledge, and acceptable tradeoffs.


A defensible process makes both the evidence considered and the role of public input visible.


Source: Chapter 6, §6.2.1.


Time: 2 minutes. Connect this to Chapters 3–5: public participation and accountability are part of sound decision processes, not extras after a technically complete decision.

title: Evidence, Framing, and Planning
text:
Plan–Do–Learn is iterative


Learning can revise the action, the objectives, or even the original problem frame.


Time: 6 minutes. Source: Chapter 6, §6.3 and Figure 6.1. Explain the image in words before discussing it. The alt text provides the text equivalent.


Source: Chapter 6, §6.3 and Figure 6.1

title: Evidence, Framing, and Planning
section: Structured decision making makes choices inspectable
text:
Structured decision making makes choices inspectable
Structured decision making makes the links explicit among:

the decision context and problem;
objectives and measurable outcomes;
management alternatives; and
predicted consequences, tradeoffs, and uncertainty.


Source: Chapter 6, §6.3.1.


Time: 3 minutes. The goal is not to make every decision slow or overly technical. It is to make the reasoning visible enough to compare alternatives and learn from results.

title: Evidence, Framing, and Planning
section: Planning turns a broad concern into a choice
text:
Planning turns a broad concern into a choice
Clear framing, objectives, alternatives, and measures.

Time: 1 minute. Transition slide.

title: Evidence, Framing, and Planning
section: Problem framing shapes the whole cycle
text:
Problem framing shapes the whole cycle
How a problem is framed influences:

who is involved;
what evidence is gathered;
which alternatives are considered; and
how success is measured.


Different frames can produce different, defensible management choices.


Time: 5 minutes. Source: Chapter 6, §§6.3–6.4. Have students apply why/who/what/how to the Puget Sound effort as a low-stakes preview.


Source: Chapter 6, §§6.3–6.4

title: Evidence, Framing, and Planning
section: A goal gives direction; objectives make it testable
text:
A goal gives direction; objectives make it testable


Goal
A broad, desired direction for management.

Objective
A specific, measurable statement of what the plan intends to achieve.


Source: Chapter 6, §6.3.2.1.


Time: 2 minutes. Students often jump directly from a broad concern to an action. This distinction makes the missing middle visible.

title: Evidence, Framing, and Planning
section: Objectives, actions, and measures are not interchangeable
text:
Objectives, actions, and measures are not interchangeable


Objective
The desired change.
Example: Improve access.

Action
What managers do.
Example: Restore a boat ramp.

Measure
Evidence of change.
Example: Reported ability to access the site.



SMART objectives are Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, and Time-bound.


Time: 7 minutes. Source: Chapter 6, §§6.3.2–6.3.2.2. Use the example only to distinguish the three terms; do not treat it as a Chapter 6 case claim.


Source: Chapter 6, §§6.3.2–6.3.2.2

title: Evidence, Framing, and Planning
section: A success metric should support a management decision
text:
A success metric should support a management decision
A useful metric is not merely easy to count. It should be:

connected to an objective;
sensitive enough to detect meaningful change;
feasible to collect and interpret; and
useful for choosing whether to continue, adjust, or replace an action.


Source: Chapter 6, §6.3.2.2.


Time: 3 minutes. A metric is part of the learning system. Ask what would be lost if a plan monitored only activity—such as number of meetings or dollars spent—rather than outcomes.

title: Evidence, Framing, and Planning
section: “Do” includes implementation, not just a decision
text:
“Do” includes implementation, not just a decision
Once an alternative is chosen, professionals must translate it into action through roles, resources, communication, partnerships, and attention to implementation conditions.

Source: Chapter 6, §6.3.3.


Time: 2 minutes. Bring forward the governance link: an action can be technically attractive but infeasible without authority, funding, partners, or an implementation plan.

title: Evidence, Framing, and Planning
text:
“Learn” requires monitoring and evaluation


Monitor
Collect information about conditions, implementation, and outcomes over time.

Evaluate
Interpret that information against objectives to decide what should change.



Learning can change an action, an objective, or the original problem frame.


Source: Chapter 6, §§6.3.4–6.3.4.2.


Time: 3 minutes. Monitoring alone is not learning. Evaluation connects observations to a decision about whether to continue or adapt.

title: Evidence, Framing, and Planning
text:
Preparing for Friday: Puget Sound
Puget Sound’s long-term recovery effort considers ecological conditions and human well-being together.

Come Friday ready to identify:

the why, who, what, and how;
one kind of evidence that matters; and
one outcome worth monitoring.



Time: 4 minutes. Source: Chapter 6, Box 6.2. Preview only; Wednesday will develop implementation, monitoring, and the Human Well-being Vital Signs.


Source: Chapter 6, Box 6.2

title: Evidence, Framing, and Planning
text:
Exit check
An agency relies only on biological information to choose an action.
Which of the four decision questions is most likely to be weakened—and why?

Time: 3 minutes. Source: Chapter 6, §6.2. Collect a short written response or pair-share. Close by previewing the Plan–Do–Learn cycle for Wednesday.


Source: Chapter 6, §6.2

title: Diversity, Equity, Inclusion, and Justice
section: Why this comes after evidence and learning
text:
Why this comes after evidence and learning
Week 4 asked how a management problem is framed, how evidence enters a plan, and how monitoring changes the next cycle.

This week asks the prior question: who is in that process, whose knowledge is taken seriously, and who is able to influence the result?

Time: 2 minutes. Source: Chapter 4, §4.2. Confirm that the Week 5 quiz covers Chapters 4 and 5 and is due Sunday at 11:59 p.m. Tell students that Monday is Chapter 4 and Wednesday is Chapter 5, and that Friday uses a new case brief they must read before class.
Pacing. Full deck is 62 minutes; the core path is 49. Five slides are marked “If time is short, skip this slide” — the “first” slide, the exclusionary-process slide, protected areas, reasserting local control, and Box 4.3. Drop from the bottom of that list up. Protect the last three slides: the pair rehearsal is the direct rehearsal for Friday item 1, and the Friday preview carries the case-brief reading expectation.


Source: Chapter 4, §4.2

title: Diversity, Equity, Inclusion, and Justice
text:
Today’s question
How do diversity, equity, inclusion, and justice shape whether a conservation decision is legitimate and durable?

Time: 1 minute. Source: Chapter 4, §4.1. Position DEIJ as part of management practice rather than as a separate policy topic layered on top of it.


Source: Chapter 4, §4.1

title: Diversity, Equity, Inclusion, and Justice
section: What you should be able to do
text:
What you should be able to do
By the end of today, you should be able to:

distinguish diversity, equity, inclusion, and justice;
explain why representation, capacity, and relevancy matter to the profession;
tell the difference between presence in a process and influence over it; and
name one guideline for working across knowledge traditions.


Time: 1 minute. Source: Chapter 4, §§4.2–4.5. These four objectives map onto the four sections of today’s class and onto the first two prompts of Friday’s application.


Source: Chapter 4, §§4.2–4.5

title: Diversity, Equity, Inclusion, and Justice
text:
Justice is a management condition
Access, influence, and recognition shape whether a conservation decision can be publicly legitimate.

Time: 1 minute. Source: Chapter 4, §4.2. Do not present DEIJ as separate from ecological outcomes or implementation.


Source: Chapter 4, §4.2

title: Diversity, Equity, Inclusion, and Justice
section: DEIJ is part of management practice
text:
DEIJ is part of management practice
DEIJ shapes:

access to land and water;
whose knowledge is recognized;
who bears costs and receives benefits; and
who has influence in public processes.


Time: 3 minutes. Source: Chapter 4, §4.2. Do not reduce DEIJ to representation alone. Ask students what each bullet would look like in a specific decision: a boat ramp, a permit draw, a comment period, a restoration contract.


Source: Chapter 4, §4.2

title: Diversity, Equity, Inclusion, and Justice
text:
Four related terms

Diversity: varying attributes within a community.
Equity: fair opportunity to engage and benefit, including attention to barriers.
Inclusion: being accepted, supported, and able to contribute.
Justice: fair practices that dismantle barriers and enable full participation.


Time: 4 minutes. Source: Chapter 4, Table 4.1. This is a text equivalent for Table 4.1. Ask students to distinguish equity from equality using only these definitions. Then ask which of the four is hardest for an agency to claim it has achieved, and why.


Source: Chapter 4, Table 4.1

title: Diversity, Equity, Inclusion, and Justice
section: The four terms are not interchangeable
text:
The four terms are not interchangeable


Institutions are sometimes criticized for emphasizing diversity and inclusion, which are more widely accepted, while avoiding the deeper questions of equity and justice that challenge existing power structures.


Time: 2 minutes. Source: Chapter 4, §4.4. This is the chapter’s own caution. Use it to explain why a demographic count is not, by itself, evidence of equity. It is a claim about institutional behavior, not about individuals.


Source: Chapter 4, §4.4

title: Diversity, Equity, Inclusion, and Justice
section: Why DEIJ matters to the profession
text:
Why DEIJ matters to the profession
Chapter 4 gives three practical reasons:

capacity: who enters, stays, and leads in the profession;
representation: whether the profession reflects the publics it serves; and
relevancy: whether conservation institutions can respond to changing communities, values, and relationships with nature.


Time: 3 minutes. Source: Chapter 4, §§4.3.1–4.3.3. Avoid treating these as recruitment-only questions. Professional composition and institutional culture affect the ability to recognize a problem, build a relationship, and act.


Source: Chapter 4, §§4.3.1–4.3.3

title: Diversity, Equity, Inclusion, and Justice
text:
A “first” is rarely enough
Numerical representation does not always translate into organizational influence.

Organizations need a critical mass of diverse voices to support innovation and belonging.
Critical mass may still fail to change direction unless people reach formal leadership roles.
Without sustained change, people experience tokenism: inclusion as a symbolic representative rather than as a full participant.


Time: 3 minutes. Source: Chapter 4, §4.4.1. The chapter names Hallie M. Daggett, Charles Young, and Deb Haaland as “firsts.” Use them to make the point that a first is a threshold, not a culture change. Do not ask students to disclose their own identity or experience.
If time is short, skip this slide. The thread survives without it.


Source: Chapter 4, §4.4.1

title: Diversity, Equity, Inclusion, and Justice
text:
Internal and external DEIJ work


Internal
Hiring, retention, leadership development, workplace culture, institutional policy. Often top-down.

External
How agencies work with publics, communities, Indigenous nations, and partners. Often bottom-up, driven by publics asserting rights, values, and knowledge.

Both face real constraints. Both are necessary.

Time: 2 minutes. Source: Chapter 4, §4.4. Friday’s case brief is an external DEIJ problem: a planning process, not a hiring process. The next two slides take up the changing legal landscape for internal DEIJ work since 2025.


Source: Chapter 4, §4.4

title: Diversity, Equity, Inclusion, and Justice
text:
The 2025 executive orders

EO 14151 and EO 14148, both signed January 20, 2025. An executive order directs the executive branch; it is not a statute or a court ruling.

Time: 4 minutes. Source: Chapter 4, §4.4; Chapter 5, §5.5.1. Set the frame out loud before advancing.
We are studying a governance mechanism and its documented effects on the profession, not evaluating the policy. No student is asked to state a position. If one volunteers, acknowledge it and return to the mechanism. If asked what you think, decline plainly — the question this course answers is what an agency can and must do, and how a professional works inside that.
The image is cropped to the document header; the surrounding site navigation is not part of the order. Read the title as data: the language an instrument uses about itself shows how the issuing authority frames the problem, which is separate from what it operationally does.
Three factual points, all mechanism and none of them an argument. Chapter 5 lists executive orders among the tools used to guide agency priorities. Civil-rights statutes — the Civil Rights Act, the Equal Pay Act — are unchanged by an order; courts, not orders, determine what the law is. And an order can be rescinded by a later one: EO 14151 itself rescinds EO 13985.
Mention the state-level parallel in one sentence so this does not read as being about one administration: Chapter 4 pairs the federal orders with Alabama’s Senate Bill 129, which prohibited DEI offices and the teaching of what the bill termed “divisive concepts,” restructuring programming at universities feeding that state’s conservation workforce. Similar bills appeared in multiple states.


Source: Chapter 4, §4.4; Chapter 5, §5.5.1

title: Diversity, Equity, Inclusion, and Justice
section: What it means for fish and wildlife
text:
What it means for fish and wildlife
Chapter 4 reports three effects on the profession: DEI-related programs were suspended across executive-branch agencies; restrictions on university programming affect the workforce pipeline; and TWS noted that layoffs of early-career professionals may hinder management of public lands and trust resources.

The profession adopted its own position first. TWS’s workforce-diversity position statement dates to October 2020, and argues from management effectiveness: engaging a greater proportion of the population lets us “more effectively manage wildlife, the ecosystems on which they depend, and the human communities that interact with them.”


Time: 4 minutes. Source: Chapter 4, §4.4; Arnett et al. 2025; Rodgers and Arnett 2025; TWS Position Statement on Workforce Diversity (2020). Keep the three effects as reported events with sources, which is what they are. Note TWS’s framing: a concern about capacity to manage trust resources is a professional argument, not a partisan one. Connect back to §4.3 — capacity, representation, relevancy. Whatever a student concludes about the orders, an agency that loses staff and pipeline has a capacity problem, and capacity determines whether it can do the work.
The 2020 date is the point of the key-idea box. The societies reached this position independently and four years earlier, on effectiveness grounds. In early 2025 TWS, the American Fisheries Society, the Society of American Foresters, and the Society for Range Management issued a joint statement warning of long-term impacts.
TWS runs this operationally: Trailblazer Grants, the Native Student Professional Development Program, an Ombuds, and working groups including Women of Wildlife and Out in the Field. Several are open to students in this room — name them, since that is the concrete reason to care.
If time allows: “You are a district biologist in 2027. Your engagement program was suspended and your partnership contacts are gone. Chapter 4 says relevancy is a condition of effective management. What do you do?”


Source: Chapter 4, §4.4; Arnett et al. 2025; Rodgers and Arnett 2025; TWS Position Statement on Workforce Diversity (2020)

title: Diversity, Equity, Inclusion, and Justice
text:
Presence is not influence
A process can include people without sharing influence.

Time: 1 minute. Source: Chapter 4, §4.4.2. This is the distinction Friday’s application turns on.


Source: Chapter 4, §4.4.2

title: Diversity, Equity, Inclusion, and Justice
text:
Presence only, or meaningful inclusion?


Presence only
People are invited, but barriers limit their participation or their knowledge has no effect on the decision.

Meaningful inclusion
Relevant publics can participate, their knowledge is recognized, and the process makes clear how their input can affect the decision.


Time: 3 minutes. Source: Chapter 4, §§4.2–4.3. Ask: “What would make an invitation insufficient?” Listen for access barriers, timing, token participation, recognition, and lack of meaningful influence. Do not require personal disclosure.


Source: Chapter 4, §§4.2–4.3

title: Diversity, Equity, Inclusion, and Justice
section: Participation has to be designed, not announced
text:
Participation has to be designed, not announced

Identify affected publics and barriers to access.
Engage early enough for input to shape the problem and the alternatives.
Explain the scope of influence and how input was used.
Build collaboration and accountability into the continuing relationship.


Time: 3 minutes. Source: Chapter 4, §4.4.2. Be clear that meaningful participation does not mean every participant receives the outcome they prefer. It means the process could have changed because of what they said.


Source: Chapter 4, §4.4.2

title: Diversity, Equity, Inclusion, and Justice
section: When a process is seen as exclusionary
text:
When a process is seen as exclusionary
Publics use many routes to assert influence: activism, protest, media, lobbying, public comment, public relations, and community organizing.


Bottom-up participation is often a response to a process that did not share influence in the first place.


Time: 2 minutes. Source: Chapter 4, §4.4.2. Frame these as governance signals rather than as obstacles. If an agency is surprised by organized opposition, that is information about the process it ran.
If time is short, skip this slide. The thread survives without it.


Source: Chapter 4, §4.4.2

title: Diversity, Equity, Inclusion, and Justice
text:
Protected areas show the stakes
Protected areas established without local consent often lack enduring public and political support. They can become:

vulnerable to PADDD — downgrading, downsizing, and degazettement; or
“paper parks” that exist on a map but lack the legitimacy needed for actual protection.


Time: 2 minutes. Source: Chapter 4, §4.4.2. Define both terms plainly. The point is that a legitimacy deficit has a material conservation consequence, not only a political one.
If time is short, skip this slide. The thread survives without it.


Source: Chapter 4, §4.4.2

title: Diversity, Equity, Inclusion, and Justice
text:
Grand Staircase–Escalante

Designated in 1996 to protect an ecologically rich landscape.
Many local communities and Indigenous nations felt they were not sufficiently consulted.
Reduced by nearly 50% in 2017 through executive action.
Critics point to the lack of local engagement and long-term political consensus as key factors.



Instructional content: Chapter 4, §4.4.2. Illustrative image: Bureau of Land Management.


Time: 3 minutes. Chapter 4, §4.4.2. Use only these case facts; do not supply external policy detail. Ask students which of the four design rules on the earlier slide appears to have been missed.
The photograph is scene-setting only and carries no instructional content — a student who cannot see it loses nothing, which is why the alt text describes the landscape rather than making an argument. Give students a beat to look at it before starting: most have never seen this landscape, and the scale is part of why the designation and the reduction both mattered so much locally.
Note for the instructor: this slide writes its footer as an explicit source-note div, because the footer has to carry the image credit as well. Keep the citation keyword out of these speaker notes or the footer filter will add a second, overlapping line.
Image provenance: the photograph is from the BLM’s Grand Staircase–Escalante page. Works of the U.S. government are in the public domain, and that page showed no separate photographer credit or licence statement when it was checked. If BLM later attributes it to a named contributor, update the footer credit to match.

title: Diversity, Equity, Inclusion, and Justice
section: The other direction: reasserting local control
text:
The other direction: reasserting local control
Communities also use protected areas to reassert authority and sustain relationships:

Grand Portage Band of Lake Superior Chippewa comanaging a national monument with the National Park Service;
transfer of the National Bison Range to the Confederated Salish and Kootenai Tribes; and
the Indigenous Circle of Experts in Canada.


Time: 2 minutes. Source: Chapter 4, §4.4.2. This prevents the section from reading as a catalogue of failure. Comanagement returns on Wednesday as a governance arrangement between sovereigns.
If time is short, skip this slide. The thread survives without it.


Source: Chapter 4, §4.4.2

title: Diversity, Equity, Inclusion, and Justice
text:
Box 4.3 — Salmon justice
For more than a century, Tribes in the Pacific Northwest have fought for the right to harvest salmon and steelhead and to sustain their communities around these fisheries.

Timber, mining, agriculture, hydropower, and commercial fishing transformed the rivers and devastated the runs.
Losses were ecological, economic, cultural, and spiritual — salmon is a primary “first food.”
Because many Tribal members eat more locally caught fish, contaminant risk can exceed what regulatory standards assume.
A 2023 federal settlement shifted control of restoration funds toward Tribal governments.


Time: 4 minutes. Source: Chapter 4, Box 4.3. Use this box to show that conservation, treaty rights, public health, and justice are one connected problem. Note the last bullet: who controls the money is a justice question and a governance question, which is Wednesday’s bridge.
If time is short, skip this slide. The thread survives without it.


Source: Chapter 4, Box 4.3

title: Diversity, Equity, Inclusion, and Justice
text:
Knowledge traditions
Disciplines, fields of study, and intergenerational ways of knowing that shape how people relate to the natural world.

Time: 1 minute. Source: Chapter 4, §4.5. Name the five the chapter treats: Indigenous knowledge systems, racial and ethnic studies, women and gender studies, queer studies, and disability studies.


Source: Chapter 4, §4.5

title: Diversity, Equity, Inclusion, and Justice
text:
The Six Rs
Many North American Indigenous knowledge systems summarize their research and relationship principles as:
respect · relationship · relevance · reciprocity · responsibility · representation

Time: 2 minutes. Source: Chapter 4, §4.5.1.1. These are practice standards for how inquiry is conducted and how relationships are maintained, not a checklist an outside researcher completes once. Connect reciprocity to the chapter’s Kimmerer example.


Source: Chapter 4, §4.5.1.1

title: Diversity, Equity, Inclusion, and Justice
section: Work across knowledge traditions with humility
text:
Work across knowledge traditions with humility


Time: 2 minutes. Source: Chapter 4, Figure 4.1. Read the alt text aloud as the text equivalent. Ask which principle matters most for Friday’s case and why.


Source: Chapter 4, Figure 4.1

title: Diversity, Equity, Inclusion, and Justice
text:
The same guidelines, in words

Identify whose work and knowledge you are building on.
Recognize the limits of your expertise.
Understand epistemology — how a tradition decides what counts as knowing.
Remember that knowledge is positional and relative.
Balance inquiry with practice.


This is a practice standard, not an invitation to treat every knowledge claim as interchangeable.

title: Diversity, Equity, Inclusion, and Justice
text:
Pair rehearsal: presence or influence?
With a partner, take one of these and decide whether it is presence only or meaningful inclusion, and say what would have to change:

A 30-day comment period on a completed draft plan.
A standing basin council that sets its own agenda but cannot decide.
A comanagement agreement that gives a sovereign partner a decision role.


Time: 5 minutes. Two minutes to decide, then hear one response for each. The useful answer names what would have to change, not just the label. Each of these three appears in Friday’s case brief as an option, so this is direct rehearsal.

title: Diversity, Equity, Inclusion, and Justice
text:
Wednesday and Friday
Wednesday: Chapter 5 — the governance machinery that decides who can share influence, and what it costs.

Before Friday: read the Week 05 Case Brief: the Cottonwood River Access and Restoration Plan. It is a separate document in the Canvas module and is required preparation.

Time: 1 minute. Source: Chapters 4–5. Say explicitly that Friday’s application is answered from the case brief, not from outside research, and that group and role assignments are already published.


Source: Chapters 4–5

title: Diversity, Equity, Inclusion, and Justice
text:
Close: a management standard
Conservation decisions are more durable when they are ecologically sound and publicly accountable to diverse publics, authorities, and contexts.

Time: 1 minute. Source: Chapter 4, §4.6. Restate the quiz deadline and the case-brief reading expectation.


Source: Chapter 4, §4.6

title: Disciplines and Paradigms
section: A wolf decision is never only a wolf decision
text:
A wolf decision is never only a wolf decision
An agency considering wolf recovery may need to ask about population dynamics. It may also need to ask about fear, livelihoods, identity, authority, and what people owe to one another and to wildlife.
Today: use disciplines as a way to ask better questions before a decision narrows too quickly.

Time: 3 minutes. Source: Chapter 7, §7.2. Start with a show of hands: What is the first question a wildlife biologist might ask? Then ask what that question cannot answer on its own. Do not suggest that biology is insufficient; it is one necessary part of a larger decision.


Source: Chapter 7, §7.2

title: Disciplines and Paradigms
section: By the end of class, you can
text:
By the end of class, you can

match a management question to a disciplinary lens;
distinguish a classic discipline from an applied field; and
explain when an interdisciplinary or transdisciplinary approach is warranted.


Time: 2 minutes. Source: Chapter 7, §7.2. These objectives move from classification to diagnosis and prepare students for Wednesday’s question about why different approaches treat different evidence as persuasive.


Source: Chapter 7, §7.2

title: Disciplines and Paradigms
section: Different lenses make different parts of a problem visible
text:
Different lenses make different parts of a problem visible
No single discipline owns a conservation problem. Each lens changes the question we can ask—and the evidence we will need.

Time: 1 minute. Source: Chapter 7, §7.2. Transition into the four classic disciplinary foundations emphasized in the chapter.


Source: Chapter 7, §7.2

title: Disciplines and Paradigms
text:
Four lenses, one wolf-recovery decision







Lens
A question it can make visible




Psychology
Why do people perceive the same risk differently?


Sociology
How do community norms and identities shape support?


Economics
Who bears costs and receives benefits under each option?


Ethics
What responsibilities and harms should guide the choice?




Source: Chapter 7, §§7.2–7.2.1.4.


Time: 4 minutes. Source: Chapter 7, §§7.2–7.2.1.4. Ask students to notice that these are not competing versions of the same question. They name different features of the decision. Keep the wolf example hypothetical; the task is to practice question selection, not argue a particular recovery policy.


Source: Chapter 7, §§7.2–7.2.1.4

title: Disciplines and Paradigms
section: Psychology asks about minds and behavior
text:
Psychology asks about minds and behavior

perceptions of a species, message, or risk;
beliefs, values, emotions, and intentions; and
why people respond differently to the same management action.

For example: Why might two residents who receive the same bear-safety message take different actions afterward?

Source: Chapter 7, §7.2.1.1.


Time: 3 minutes. Source: Chapter 7, §7.2.1.1. Preview Chapter 8 without teaching its full behavior frameworks today. Emphasize that psychology can study individuals and groups, but its central unit of analysis is often the mind and behavior.


Source: Chapter 7, §7.2.1.1

title: Disciplines and Paradigms
section: Sociology asks about relationships and institutions
text:
Sociology asks about relationships and institutions

social norms, identities, and community relationships;
how traditions and opportunities are passed on; and
how institutions and trust shape conservation outcomes.

For example: How might a hunting tradition be sustained—or interrupted—across generations in one community?

Source: Chapter 7, §7.2.1.2.


Time: 3 minutes. Source: Chapter 7, §7.2.1.2. Contrast this with psychology: instead of asking why one person decides to hunt, sociology can ask how family, community, place, and institutions make that decision more or less possible.


Source: Chapter 7, §7.2.1.2

title: Disciplines and Paradigms
section: Economics makes scarcity and distribution explicit
text:
Economics makes scarcity and distribution explicit
Economics is not simply “putting a dollar value on nature.” It asks how limited resources are allocated, what incentives people face, and how costs and benefits are distributed across time and among people.
For example: Who pays for wetland restoration, who benefits, and what changes if landowners face a different incentive?

Source: Chapter 7, §7.2.1.3.


Time: 3 minutes. Source: Chapter 7, §7.2.1.3. Foreshadow Week 9. Make clear that an economic comparison can inform a decision without deciding what is fair or morally acceptable.


Source: Chapter 7, §7.2.1.3

title: Disciplines and Paradigms
section: Ethics addresses the question evidence cannot settle alone
text:
Ethics addresses the question evidence cannot settle alone
Data can help estimate likely outcomes. They cannot, by themselves, decide what outcomes ought to matter most.

Is lethal control justified to protect an endangered species?
What is owed to people living with a management burden?
What obligations do present people have to future generations?


Source: Chapter 7, §7.2.1.4.


Time: 3 minutes. Source: Chapter 7, §7.2.1.4. Keep ethics distinct from personal preference. Ethical reasoning gives a disciplined way to examine propositions about right and wrong; it does not eliminate disagreement.


Source: Chapter 7, §7.2.1.4

title: Disciplines and Paradigms
section: Some fields turn knowledge into action
text:
Some fields turn knowledge into action
Applied fields help agencies implement, communicate, regulate, fund, and evaluate decisions in the settings where conservation actually happens.

Time: 1 minute. Source: Chapter 7, §7.2.2. This is a bridge: the first set of lenses helps explain a problem; applied fields help make a response workable.


Source: Chapter 7, §7.2.2

title: Disciplines and Paradigms
section: A strong decision needs more than a good explanation
text:
A strong decision needs more than a good explanation



Field
What it contributes to practice




Education
skills, learning, and environmental literacy


Law
authority, constraints, and enforceable rules


Planning
land use, infrastructure, and competing needs


Public administration
accountability, budgets, and coordination


Business
finance, organization, and program delivery




Source: Chapter 7, §7.2.2.


Time: 4 minutes. Source: Chapter 7, §7.2.2. Ask: Which field becomes essential after an agency has selected an alternative? Answer: often several at once. Connect to Week 4 implementation—an adopted plan still needs authority, resources, staff capacity, and public accountability.


Source: Chapter 7, §7.2.2

title: Disciplines and Paradigms
section: Arts and humanities are evidence about meaning—not decoration
text:
Arts and humanities are evidence about meaning—not decoration
Stories, images, history, and cultural expression can reveal how people attach meaning to a species or place. They can also communicate consequences in ways a technical report may not.
That does not mean substituting a moving image for evidence. It means asking what a solely technical account is unable to hear or convey.

Source: Chapter 7, §7.2.3 and Box 7.1.


Time: 3 minutes. Source: Chapter 7, §7.2.3 and Box 7.1. Use the chapter’s examples of visual art, illustration, and ecological art to show that art can educate, change imagination, and sometimes materially contribute to habitat. Ask students for a conservation image that changed what they noticed.


Source: Chapter 7, §7.2.3 and Box 7.1

title: Disciplines and Paradigms
section: When disciplines meet, the work changes
text:
When disciplines meet, the work changes
Complex decisions often require scientists to connect methods—and to work with the people who will live with the decision.

Time: 1 minute. Source: Chapter 7, §7.2.4. Transition from a collection of lenses to the degree of integration among them.


Source: Chapter 7, §7.2.4

title: Disciplines and Paradigms
section: Interdisciplinary is not the same as transdisciplinary
text:
Interdisciplinary is not the same as transdisciplinary

Multidisciplinary: several fields address one problem side by side.
Interdisciplinary: fields integrate concepts, theories, or methods.
Transdisciplinary: scientific fields work with practitioners, decision makers, and resource users to define, interpret, and apply the work.

The key question is not “How many disciplines are present?” but “Who helped shape the problem and how are their insights connected?”

Source: Chapter 7, §7.2.4.


Time: 4 minutes. Source: Chapter 7, §7.2.4. Use deer management as the chapter example: ecology, survey research, economics, and spatial modeling can be integrated. Then ask what changes when landowners, hunters, Tribal governments, and agency staff help define the problem from the outset.


Source: Chapter 7, §7.2.4

title: Disciplines and Paradigms
section: Quick practice: build the question set
text:
Quick practice: build the question set
Scenario: A town wants to reduce road collisions with deer near new housing.
With a partner, write two questions the project team must answer:

one question a biological or spatial lens would ask; and
one question from a human-dimensions lens.

Then name one field or partner that should be involved before the team chooses an alternative.

Time: 6 minutes. Source: Chapter 7, §§7.2–7.2.4. Circulate and press students to write questions rather than solutions. Debrief by sorting examples: risk perception, commuting patterns, property-owner costs, development rules, responsibility, and wildlife movement all belong in a fuller problem frame.


Source: Chapter 7, §§7.2–7.2.4

title: Disciplines and Paradigms
section: Close: choose the question before choosing the method
text:
Close: choose the question before choosing the method
A survey, interview, cost analysis, map, or public meeting is not inherently the right tool. The useful tool is the one that matches a clearly framed question and an accountable decision process.
Wednesday: Why can two rigorous teams study the same issue and still treat different kinds of evidence as convincing?

Source: Chapter 7, §§7.2–7.3.


Time: 2 minutes. Source: Chapter 7, §§7.2–7.3. Collect one question from two or three pairs. Explain that Wednesday will make the assumptions under those choices visible: reality, knowledge, method, and values.


Source: Chapter 7, §§7.2–7.3

title: Psychology and Human Behavior
text:
“They just need to care more”
You will hear this sentence in a management meeting. It is almost always wrong — not because caring is irrelevant, but because the people in question usually already care.
This week asks what else has to be true before a person acts.

Time: 2 minutes. Source: Chapter 8, §8.2. Ask for a show of hands: who has been told to do something they already believed in, and did not do it? That is the whole week in one question.
Pacing. Full deck is 46 minutes; the core path is 43. Slides marked “If time is short, skip this slide” are the drop list: the “five jobs” slide. Protect the person-and-situation slide and the worked contrast — they are the week’s core and the rehearsal for Friday item 2.


Source: Chapter 8, §8.2

title: Psychology and Human Behavior
text:
Today’s question
What does psychology add once we already know that people support a conservation goal?

Time: 1 minute. Source: Chapter 8, §8.2. Position psychology as diagnostic: it tells you which part of the chain is broken, which determines which intervention could possibly work.


Source: Chapter 8, §8.2

title: Psychology and Human Behavior
section: What you should be able to do
text:
What you should be able to do
By the end of today, you should be able to:

distinguish cognition, conation, and affect;
explain the person and the situation as two interacting lenses;
explain the cognitive hierarchy from values to specific behavior; and
state the specificity principle and why it matters for prediction.


Time: 1 minute. Source: Chapter 8, §§8.3–8.4.1. Wednesday adds the frameworks that turn this diagnosis into a strategy.


Source: Chapter 8, §§8.3–8.4.1

title: Psychology and Human Behavior
text:
What psychology is for
It connects individual thought and behavior to practical management problems.

Time: 1 minute. Source: Chapter 8, §8.2.


Source: Chapter 8, §8.2

title: Psychology and Human Behavior
section: Five jobs psychology does in management
text:
Five jobs psychology does in management

Designing interventions — targeting the actual drivers of action.
Enhancing participation — uncovering what motivates or discourages different publics.
Managing conflict — understanding the roots of conflict among people, groups, and institutions.
Contextual planning — making plans relevant to local communities.
Informing decisions — cognitive biases, emotions, bounded rationality, and uncertainty.


Time: 3 minutes. Source: Chapter 8, §8.2. Each of these connects forward to a later chapter: participation to Chapter 13, conflict to Chapter 18, decisions to Chapter 6. Psychology is not a detour from management; it is the diagnostic layer under it.
If time is short, skip this slide. The thread survives without it.


Source: Chapter 8, §8.2

title: Psychology and Human Behavior
text:
A caution before we start
Most classic disciplines, psychology included, emerged within Western cultures and ways of knowing. There is often an implicit assumption that those concepts apply universally.

Cultural relevance: the degree to which a practice, intervention, or program is tailored to the specific cultural backgrounds, values, and experiences of a community.


Time: 3 minutes. Source: Chapter 8, §8.2.1. Cross-cultural psychology tests whether dominant Western concepts hold in other contexts. Connect back to Week 6’s treatment of Indigenous ways of knowing: the question of whether a construct travels is an epistemological question, not a translation problem.


Source: Chapter 8, §8.2.1

title: Psychology and Human Behavior
text:
Three components of mental life
Cognition · conation · affect

Time: 1 minute. Source: Chapter 8, §8.3.


Source: Chapter 8, §8.3

title: Psychology and Human Behavior
text:
Cognition, conation, affect








Component
What it is
A question that reveals it




Cognition
Mental processes: perception, reasoning, memory
“Do you think draining your boat makes a difference?”


Conation
Motivational and volitional drive: will, intent, striving
“Do you intend to do it on your next trip?”


Affect
The experience of emotions and feelings
“How do you feel when you see the agency’s sign?”



These interact to form internal states — beliefs and attitudes — which then appear as observable decisions and actions.

Time: 6 minutes. Source: Chapter 8, §8.3. Spend the time here; students routinely collapse all three into “attitude.” Work an example across all three columns. Stress that affect is a relative newcomer to the field and is not a softer version of cognition.


Source: Chapter 8, §8.3

title: Psychology and Human Behavior
text:
The person and the situation


The person
Intrapersonal factors. Internal explanations for thought and behavior.

The situation
Interpersonal and situational factors. The social or biophysical structures that explain thought and behavior.


The person and the situation are inseparable. Social and cognitive psychology explain behavior by analyzing how the two interact.


Time: 5 minutes. Source: Chapter 8, §8.3. This is the single most important slide of the week. The failure mode in management is locating the whole problem in the person — “they don’t care,” “they’re lazy” — when the situation produced the behavior. The opposite failure is real too: removing every barrier and being surprised that nothing changed.


Source: Chapter 8, §8.3

title: Psychology and Human Behavior
text:
A worked contrast
A landowner wants to secure bear attractants but has nowhere secure to store them.

Diagnosing this as a values problem produces a brochure.


Diagnosing it as a situational constraint produces storage.



The same observed behavior — attractants left out — supports two completely different interventions. Only one of them can work.



Time: 4 minutes. Source: Chapter 8, §8.3. Reveal the fragments one at a time and let students commit before the third. This is the direct rehearsal for Friday’s item 2.


Source: Chapter 8, §8.3

title: Psychology and Human Behavior
text:
The cognitive hierarchy
From abstract and stable to specific and situational.

Time: 1 minute. Source: Chapter 8, §8.4.1 and Box 8.5.


Source: Chapter 8, §8.4.1 and Box 8.5

title: Psychology and Human Behavior
text:
From values to behavior
values → value orientations → attitudes and norms → behavioral intention → behavior

Values are few, abstract, and stable across a life.
Value orientations are patterns among basic beliefs — the link between abstract values and specific cognitions.
Attitudes and norms are specific to an object or an action.
Intention is the most immediate predictor of behavior.


Time: 5 minutes. Source: Chapter 8, §8.4.1 and Box 8.5. Wildlife value orientations are the best-known application in this field. Draw the hierarchy as a pyramid: many specific cognitions rest on few abstract values, which is why values change slowly and attitudes do not.


Source: Chapter 8, §8.4.1 and Box 8.5

title: Psychology and Human Behavior
text:
The specificity principle
Correlations between variables are larger when the variables correspond in target, action, context, and time.

Wildlife value orientations predict general acceptability of hunting well.
They predict archery hunting [action] a white-tailed deer [target] in a suburban neighborhood [context] in fall 2027 [time] far less well.


If you want to predict a specific behavior, you must measure something equally specific.


Time: 5 minutes. Source: Chapter 8, Box 8.5. This is the conceptual root of TACT, which arrives Wednesday. The Anchorage study found exactly this pattern: stronger correlations between general orientations and general actions than between general orientations and specific actions. The management implication is blunt — a values survey cannot tell you whether a particular rule will be followed.


Source: Chapter 8, Box 8.5

title: Psychology and Human Behavior
text:
Pair rehearsal: sort the evidence
With a partner, label each as cognition, conation, or affect:

“I don’t think one person draining a boat matters.”
“I feel blamed every time I read one of those signs.”
“I plan to do it next time I’m out.”
“Invasive mussels would ruin this lake.”


Time: 5 minutes. Source: Chapter 8, §8.3. Answers: 1 cognition (a belief about efficacy), 2 affect, 3 conation (intention), 4 cognition. Item 1 is the one students miss — it sounds like apathy and is actually a belief. Every one of these appears in Friday’s case brief.


Source: Chapter 8, §8.3

title: Psychology and Human Behavior
text:
Wednesday and Friday
Wednesday: the frameworks — reasoned action and TACT, collective action and norms, emotions, motivation and satisfaction.
Before Friday: read the Week 07 Case Brief: The Thornapple Lake Decontamination Problem. It is a separate document in the Canvas module and is required preparation.

Time: 2 minutes. Source: Chapter 8, §§8.4–8.4.5. Say explicitly that Friday is answered from the case brief, not from outside research, and that group and role assignments are already published.


Source: Chapter 8, §§8.4–8.4.5

title: Psychology and Human Behavior
text:
Close

Psychology does not tell you what people should do. It tells you which part of the chain between belief and action is actually broken — which is what determines whether your intervention has any chance.


Time: 1 minute. Source: Chapter 8, §8.5. Restate the quiz deadline and the case-brief reading expectation.


Source: Chapter 8, §8.5

title: Sociology and Social Change
section: Last week we looked inside the person
text:
Last week we looked inside the person
Psychology asked what a person believes, intends, and feels, and what the situation in front of them allows.
This week the unit of analysis changes. Sociology asks about the patterns that exist beyond any one person — and that shape what any individual can believe, intend, or do.

Time: 2 minutes. Source: Chapter 9, §9.2. Be explicit that this is not a correction of psychology. It is a different level of explanation, and the two are complementary.
Pacing. Full deck is 50 minutes; the core path is 42. Slides marked “If time is short, skip this slide” are the drop list: the “applied” slide and social order/social change. Protect troubles-and-issues and the pair rehearsal — both are Friday item 1.


Source: Chapter 9, §9.2

title: Sociology and Social Change
text:
Today’s question
When thousands of people give the same individual reason, what are we actually looking at?

Time: 1 minute. Source: Chapter 9, §9.3.2. This is the troubles-versus-issues question, and it is the spine of Friday’s item 1.


Source: Chapter 9, §9.3.2

title: Sociology and Social Change
section: What you should be able to do
text:
What you should be able to do
By the end of today, you should be able to:

distinguish structure and agency, and explain why you need both;
define a social fact and distinguish a private trouble from a public issue;
explain social construction and give a fish-and-wildlife example; and
define social order and social change.


Time: 1 minute. Source: Chapter 9, §§9.3.1–9.3.5. Wednesday adds the three theoretical perspectives and the core concepts of socialization, community, and stratification.


Source: Chapter 9, §§9.3.1–9.3.5

title: Sociology and Social Change
text:
Structure and agency
Society shapes people. People reshape society.

Time: 1 minute. Source: Chapter 9, §9.3.1.


Source: Chapter 9, §9.3.1

title: Sociology and Social Change
text:
Two words, one relationship


Structure
The stable, patterned relationships among societal elements that influence human action: institutions, roles, norms.

Agency
The capacity of individuals to act independently and make choices.


Structuration: people’s interactions create and renegotiate structures, while individuals act within the contexts those structures produce.


Time: 5 minutes. Source: Chapter 9, §9.3.1. Giddens’ point is mutual dependence, not a compromise between two positions. Do not let students translate it as “some of each.”


Source: Chapter 9, §9.3.1

title: Sociology and Social Change
text:
The river and its banks
A river’s banks guide its flow.
The flow gradually reshapes the banks.

Society influences human behavior while individuals actively reshape society.


Time: 3 minutes. Source: Chapter 9, §9.3.1. This is the chapter’s own analogy and it is the fastest way to recover the concept when a group collapses into pure structure or pure choice on Friday. Ask: what would it mean to say the river “chose” its course? What would it mean to say the banks are the whole story?


Source: Chapter 9, §9.3.1

title: Sociology and Social Change
text:
Applied: why did participation change?
A sociologist asks structural questions:

Has urbanization made the landscape harder to access?
Have rural communities — traditionally a primary source of social support for hunting — declined in population?
Have those areas changed in character, even where headcount held?


Time: 4 minutes. Source: Chapter 9, §9.3.1 and Box 9.1. Box 9.1 notes that urbanization is the demographic trend most strongly associated with reducing participation, and that most demographic trends dampen it. Note the third bullet: character can change while population does not. Friday’s Exhibit A is built on exactly that distinction.
If time is short, skip this slide. The thread survives without it.


Source: Chapter 9, §9.3.1 and Box 9.1

title: Sociology and Social Change
text:
Social facts
Values, norms, and structures that exist outside any one person.

Time: 1 minute. Source: Chapter 9, §9.3.2.


Source: Chapter 9, §9.3.2

title: Sociology and Social Change
text:
Durkheim’s move
The decision to die by suicide is intensely personal. Yet rates vary enormously across places, groups, and eras.

An explanation that works only at the individual level cannot explain why the rate differs. Durkheim found social support to be a strong predictor of aggregate rates.


Time: 4 minutes. Source: Chapter 9, §9.3.2. Handle this example with care and keep it brief and analytic. The methodological point is what matters: a purely individual explanation cannot account for variation in an aggregate rate. That move is the foundation of the discipline.


Source: Chapter 9, §9.3.2

title: Sociology and Social Change
text:
Troubles and issues
C. Wright Mills:


Troubles
Private experiences. One person’s schedule got busier. One person lost a place to hunt.

Issues
The same troubles, when they become widespread across a population — and point to structural change.


Time: 6 minutes. Source: Chapter 9, §9.3.2. Work the chapter’s own example: a survey shows hunters quit because of “no time” or “nowhere to go.” On the surface, individual troubles. But their broad distribution asks different questions — has leisure time declined generally? has land conversion or posting increased in certain regions? This is precisely Friday’s item 1, and the case brief supplies the county data that converts one into the other.


Source: Chapter 9, §9.3.2

title: Sociology and Social Change
text:
Social construction
Concepts created through human interaction and maintained by collective agreement.

Time: 1 minute. Source: Chapter 9, §9.3.3.


Source: Chapter 9, §9.3.3

title: Sociology and Social Change
text:
Game fish and rough fish
Both are real animals. The categories are social constructs.

“Game fish” are constructed as desirable, so policy promotes them: creel, length, and gear limits.
“Rough fish,” often native species, are constructed as less valuable — so many go unregulated entirely: no creel, bag, or gear limit.


Saying a category is socially constructed does not mean it is imaginary. It means the agreement is what produces the regulation.


Time: 6 minutes. Source: Chapter 9, §9.3.3. This is the best example in the chapter because the management consequence is so concrete. Also cover “endangered”: we designate a species endangered because we decided a population has fallen below a socially acceptable threshold warranting intervention. The threshold is a social judgment applied to a biological measurement.


Source: Chapter 9, §9.3.3

title: Sociology and Social Change
text:
What is not socially constructed
Gravity. Temperature. Thermodynamics.

Professionals constantly negotiate the tension between biophysical realities that no belief can alter and social constructions that determine what we do about them.


Time: 3 minutes. Source: Chapter 9, §9.3.3. Insert this deliberately. Students either over-apply social construction to everything or dismiss it as relativism; this slide forecloses both. “Wilderness,” by contrast, is a construct carrying cultural, symbolic, and political significance — the same physical place is viewed very differently by different people and cultures.


Source: Chapter 9, §9.3.3

title: Sociology and Social Change
text:
Social order and social change
Social order: the structures, institutions, facts, and constructs that maintain stability — and which can also produce inequalities of status, role, and position.
Social change: transformation of basic social structures and institutions over time, often originating in economics, politics, technology, or natural realities.

Time: 4 minutes. Source: Chapter 9, §§9.3.4–9.3.5. Give the chapter’s management example of social order: traditional agency funding structures often prioritize license buyers, positioning other publics lower in a perceived hierarchy — which influences whose interests are included. That connects directly back to Week 5’s governance and funding discussion. For social change, use the 1970s environmental movement: culture, politics, and natural realities shifting at once.
If time is short, skip this slide. The thread survives without it.


Source: Chapter 9, §§9.3.4–9.3.5

title: Sociology and Social Change
text:
Pair rehearsal: trouble or issue?
With a partner, decide which each is, and name the structural question you would ask:

“I lost my hunting spot when the neighbor sold the farm.”
63% of lapsed hunters in a county say they have “nowhere to go.”
“I don’t have time anymore.”
Commuting over 30 minutes rose from 19% to 46% of county residents.


Time: 5 minutes. Source: Chapter 9, §9.3.2. Items 1 and 3 are troubles as stated; 2 and 4 are the same content as issues. The useful answer names the structural question — who sold, to whom, and why did that pattern accelerate? All four figures appear in Friday’s case brief.

Close

When thousands of people give the same private reason, the reason has stopped being private. That is the moment a management problem becomes a sociological one.
